scope_note: Every LLM inference engine and serving runtime that matters in 2026 — local single-user engines, high-throughput multi-user serving engines, engines built around one quantization format, and hardware-platform-specific engines — on the axes that actually decide a project: which model formats and quantizations it loads, which hardware it runs on, and whether it exposes an OpenAI-compatible API.
method_note: Nothing here is benchmarked by OpenGauntlet's judge pipeline. Most figures come from primary sources — vendor docs, repositories, and papers. Two rows, vLLM and SGLang, are the one exception on this whole site: their `benchmarks` field cites a first-party comparison OpenGauntlet ran on its own hardware (docs/serving-backends.md), not a vendor claim relayed from elsewhere — marked `verification: verified` rather than `vendor-claim` for that reason. This is a growing survey; see gaps below for what has not yet been added.

systems.name: vLLM
systems.price_note: Free / self-host (open-source; usage cost is whatever hardware you run it on)
systems.model_formats: Safetensors natively (FP8, NVFP4, BF16/FP16, AWQ, GPTQ); no native GGUF support
systems.hardware_support: NVIDIA CUDA (broadest coverage), AMD ROCm, Intel Gaudi, Google TPU, AWS Neuron; multi-GPU tensor and pipeline parallelism
systems.api_note: OpenAI-compatible /v1 endpoint (chat completions, completions, embeddings)
systems.runs_on: Docker container or bare Python server process; the default serving backend for this project's own benchmark pipeline
systems.best_for: The default choice for self-hosted high-throughput serving of safetensors models, when broad architecture coverage matters more than squeezing out the last ~19% of concurrent throughput a narrower-coverage alternative might offer.
systems.watch: Cold start is measured at 376s on a 35B MoE model on this project's own hardware — substantially slower to first request than SGLang's 151s on the same model, though warm single-stream decode is identical between the two (a property of the model and memory bandwidth, not the server).
systems.standout: The architecture-coverage default in this project's own serving pipeline — loads every candidate model architecture the project has needed (7 of 7 in an internal probe), where the fastest alternative (SGLang) loads 4 of 7.
systems.architecture: PagedAttention KV-cache management with continuous batching
systems.throughput_note: On this project's own hardware (NVIDIA GB10, sm_121): concurrency-16 aggregate throughput 208.6 tok/s on a 35B MoE model at FP8. See benchmarks for full figures and conditions.
systems.multi_gpu: Yes — tensor parallel and pipeline parallel
systems.benchmarks: OpenGauntlet's own benchmark (docs/serving-backends.md), same model (qwen3.5-35b-a3b-fp8, 35B MoE, 256 experts/8 active, FP8) served identically by both vLLM and SGLang on NVIDIA GB10 (sm_121): cold start 376s; TTFT@512 tok 217ms (cold); TTFT@2048 481ms; TTFT@8192 1625ms; single-stream decode 44.8-46.5 tok/s; one 8-turn conversation 29.1s; concurrency-4 aggregate 105.2 tok/s; concurrency-8 149.2 tok/s; concurrency-16 208.6 tok/s; amortised 6.14s/conversation at concurrency 16. Architecture coverage probed against ModelRegistry in each image: vLLM 7/7 candidate architectures, SGLang 4/7.
systems.adoption: The most widely deployed open-source LLM serving engine as of this writing, per its own project documentation and broad ecosystem integration (Hugging Face, most major model releases ship day-one vLLM support).
systems.verification_note: Licence read off the repository LICENSE file. Hardware-support and api_note claims read off the project's own documentation (docs/serving-backends.md). Throughput/latency figures in `benchmarks` are OpenGauntlet's own first-party measurement on its own hardware, not a vendor claim.

systems.name: SGLang
systems.price_note: Free / self-host (open-source; usage cost is whatever hardware you run it on)
systems.model_formats: Safetensors natively (FP8, NVFP4, BF16/FP16, AWQ, GPTQ); no native GGUF support
systems.hardware_support: NVIDIA CUDA, AMD ROCm; multi-GPU tensor parallelism
systems.api_note: OpenAI-compatible /v1 endpoint
systems.runs_on: Docker container or bare Python server process; an opt-in fast path in this project's own serving pipeline for the architectures it supports
systems.best_for: Self-hosted serving of a model whose architecture SGLang supports, when faster cold start and higher concurrent throughput matter more than the broadest possible architecture coverage.
systems.watch: Loads only 4 of 7 architectures on this project's own candidate-model probe (missing Gemma4* and DeepseekV4 support at time of measurement) — coverage is a hard gate, not a speed trade-off, so a model SGLang cannot load is not usable here at any speed regardless of how favorable its other numbers are.
systems.standout: 2.4x faster cold start than vLLM (151s vs 376s) and 13.7x faster warm prefill TTFT at 8192 tokens (116ms vs 1598ms) on identical hardware and model, measured by this project directly rather than relayed from either vendor.
systems.architecture: RadixAttention KV-cache reuse with continuous batching
systems.throughput_note: On this project's own hardware (NVIDIA GB10, sm_121): concurrency-16 aggregate throughput 248.2 tok/s on the same 35B MoE model at FP8 — 19% higher than vLLM's 208.6 tok/s under identical conditions. See benchmarks for full figures.
systems.benchmarks: OpenGauntlet's own benchmark (docs/serving-backends.md), same model (qwen3.5-35b-a3b-fp8, 35B MoE, 256 experts/8 active, FP8) served identically by both vLLM and SGLang on NVIDIA GB10 (sm_121): cold start 151s; TTFT@512 tok 279ms (cold); TTFT@2048 493ms; TTFT@8192 1567ms cold / 116ms warm (13.7x faster warm than vLLM); single-stream decode 44.2-46.0 tok/s; one 8-turn conversation 29.7s; concurrency-4 aggregate 113.8 tok/s; concurrency-8 171.0 tok/s; concurrency-16 248.2 tok/s; amortised 5.16s/conversation at concurrency 16. Architecture coverage probed against ModelRegistry: SGLang 4/7 candidate architectures vs vLLM's 7/7.
systems.adoption: Adopted specifically for its measured speed advantage on architectures it supports, per this project's own serving-backend decision record.
systems.verification_note: Licence read off the repository LICENSE file. A prior internal pass concluded SGLang could not run on this project's specific GPU (compute capability 12.1) from a torch import warning about unsupported capability ranges — that conclusion was corrected after direct testing: the warning was not a failure, and SGLang serves models on this hardware at full speed via sm100 kernels. Throughput/latency figures in `benchmarks` are OpenGauntlet's own first-party measurement, not a vendor claim.

systems.name: llama.cpp
systems.model_formats: GGUF is the only format the runtime loads natively; safetensors/PyTorch checkpoints must be converted to GGUF first via the project's conversion scripts
systems.hardware_support: CPU (BLAS/BLIS/ZenDNN, AVX/AVX2/AVX512/AMX x86, ARM NEON/Accelerate, RISC-V RVV); CUDA (NVIDIA); HIP (AMD/ROCm); Metal (Apple Silicon); Vulkan; SYCL (Intel GPU); OpenCL (Adreno); MUSA (Moore Threads); CANN (Ascend NPU); WebGPU and OpenVINO backends in progress
systems.api_note: OpenAI-compatible /v1 endpoint via the bundled llama-server, plus its own native completion/embedding endpoints
systems.runs_on: Bare process (CLI + llama-server binary); also an embeddable C/C++ library used inside most other tools in this table
systems.best_for: The reference GGUF runtime with the widest hardware/backend coverage and full control over build flags
systems.watch: GGUF is the only format this runtime loads natively — safetensors/PyTorch checkpoints must be converted to GGUF first via the project's own conversion scripts before llama.cpp can run them.
systems.standout: The foundational C/C++ inference engine that nearly every other tool in this table wraps, forks, or converts models for
systems.architecture: Plain C/C++ with no external dependencies, built on the GGML tensor library
systems.multi_gpu: Yes — layer split (default, low interconnect bandwidth needed), row split (legacy, PCIe-heavy, discouraged), and an experimental tensor-parallel split mode
systems.quantisation: Native GGUF quantization from 1.5-bit through 8-bit integer (Q2_K–Q8_0, IQ-series importance-matrix quants, etc.)
systems.adoption: 123k+ GitHub stars, 21k+ forks; embedded inside Ollama, KoboldCpp, LM Studio, GPT4All, Jan, LocalAI, llamafile, text-generation-webui and many others
systems.verification_note: Confirmed against the official ggml-org/llama.cpp GitHub README, docs/build.md and docs/multi-gpu.md

systems.name: LM Studio
systems.licence: Proprietary EULA (the bundled mlx-engine component is separately MIT-licensed)
systems.price_note: Free for personal and internal business use; EULA forbids resale/SaaS use of the app itself
systems.model_formats: GGUF (via a bundled llama.cpp engine) and MLX (via a bundled Apple MLX engine on Apple Silicon), switchable per model from the UI
systems.hardware_support: Apple Silicon M1–M4 via Metal/MLX; Windows x64 (AVX2 required) and ARM64 (Snapdragon X Elite); Linux x64/ARM64; ~4GB+ VRAM recommended for GPU offload, CPU-only inference also works via llama.cpp
systems.api_note: OpenAI-compatible REST server at http://localhost:1234/v1 (chat, completions, embeddings, responses); also a headless daemon (llmster) and TypeScript/Python SDKs
systems.runs_on: Desktop app (GUI) for macOS/Windows/Linux; llmster headless daemon for servers/CI
systems.best_for: Non-technical users who want a polished chat GUI plus a local OpenAI-compatible server without touching a terminal
systems.watch: Closed-source proprietary app under a restrictive EULA — no reverse engineering, redistribution, or SaaS use permitted, and there is no public source to audit
systems.architecture: Proprietary desktop shell wrapping the open-source llama.cpp and MLX engines
systems.verification_note: Model formats and hardware confirmed via LM Studio's own blog and system-requirements docs; API surface confirmed via lmstudio.ai/docs; EULA terms confirmed via lmstudio.ai/terms

systems.name: LocalAI
systems.model_formats: GGUF, safetensors, plus whatever its 60+ pluggable backends load (diffusers, MLX-VLM, etc.); models pulled from Hugging Face, Ollama registries, or OCI registries
systems.hardware_support: CUDA 12/13 (NVIDIA) incl. Jetson L4T ARM64, ROCm (AMD), oneAPI/SYCL (Intel), Metal (Apple Silicon), Vulkan, or CPU-only with no GPU required
systems.api_note: Drop-in OpenAI-, Anthropic-, and ElevenLabs-compatible API covering chat, embeddings, vision, function calling, and realtime speech-to-speech
systems.runs_on: Docker/Podman containers (CPU and GPU images), a bare binary, or Kubernetes; backends are pulled on-demand as separate OCI images
systems.best_for: Self-hosters who want one OpenAI-compatible gateway in front of text, image, speech, and embedding models simultaneously, not just LLM chat
systems.watch: Backends for its 60+ pluggable capabilities are pulled on-demand as separate OCI images at runtime rather than bundled — the specific backend a model needs may require an extra download the first time you use it, and total disk footprint grows with how many backends you touch.
systems.standout: One OpenAI-compatible gateway spanning text, image, speech-to-text, and TTS across 60+ pluggable backends
systems.architecture: Go, modular backend-per-OCI-image design
systems.multi_gpu: Automatic multi-GPU model fitting (via llama.cpp) plus VRAM-aware routing in distributed mode
systems.verification_note: Confirmed against mudler/LocalAI GitHub README

systems.name: llamafile
systems.model_formats: GGUF, embedded directly inside the executable or loaded externally
systems.hardware_support: CPU on virtually any architecture via Cosmopolitan Libc (the same binary runs on Windows/macOS/Linux/BSD); Metal on Apple Silicon; CUDA on NVIDIA; AMD GPU support via the llama.cpp integration
systems.api_note: Runs the llama.cpp server underneath, so exposes the same OpenAI-compatible /v1 endpoint
systems.runs_on: A single self-contained executable — no install, no dependencies
systems.best_for: Distributing one model plus runtime as a single double-clickable file with zero install, ideal for air-gapped or non-technical handoff
systems.watch: Portability comes from embedding the model weights directly inside the executable via Cosmopolitan Libc — a "single file" therefore bundles the full model, so shipping an update means re-distributing the whole file rather than swapping a small binary, and only GGUF is supported, the same hard format gate as upstream llama.cpp.
systems.standout: One binary IS the model — a single file runs identically on Windows, macOS, Linux, and BSD with no install step, via Cosmopolitan Libc
systems.architecture: llama.cpp compiled with Cosmopolitan Libc into an Actually Portable Executable
systems.verification_note: Confirmed against Mozilla-Ocho/llamafile GitHub README

systems.name: ik_llama.cpp
systems.model_formats: GGUF, plus additional quant types it defines itself (Trellis IQ1_KT–IQ4_KT, IQK IQ2_K–IQ6_K, MXFP4) layered on top of the standard llama.cpp quant set
systems.hardware_support: CPU (AVX2+ x86, ARM_NEON+), CUDA (Turing or newer NVIDIA); explicitly does not support ROCm, Vulkan, Metal, older NVIDIA cards, or pre-AVX2 CPUs; Android via Termux added April 2025
systems.api_note: Same OpenAI-compatible llama-server as mainline llama.cpp, since this is a source fork
systems.runs_on: Bare process (CLI + server binary), same model as llama.cpp
systems.best_for: Squeezing extra tokens/sec out of large MoE models (DeepSeek-class) on hybrid CPU+CUDA rigs, via quant types mainline llama.cpp doesn't ship
systems.watch: A one-person fork last synced with upstream llama.cpp in August 2024 — it has diverged since, so newer mainline features/model support may lag or need manual porting; no ROCm/Vulkan/Metal, so it only helps CUDA+CPU users
systems.standout: SOTA-claiming quantization types (Trellis/IQK) and MoE inference optimizations mainline llama.cpp doesn't have, aimed at running huge MoE models on CPU+CUDA hybrid rigs
systems.architecture: C/C++ fork of llama.cpp/ggml
systems.quantisation: Extended GGUF quant set beyond mainline llama.cpp (Trellis, IQK, MXFP4)
systems.verification_note: Confirmed against ikawrakow/ik_llama.cpp GitHub README

systems.name: KTransformers
systems.model_formats: GGUF and safetensors, with INT4/INT8 quantized weights
systems.hardware_support: NVIDIA CUDA, AMD ROCm, Intel Arc (XPU), Ascend NPU, plus x86 CPU with AMX/AVX-512/AVX2 for the CPU half of its heterogeneous CPU+GPU inference
systems.api_note: Integrates with SGLang for a production-style serving API
systems.runs_on: Bare process/Python library; requires assembling matched CPU+GPU hardware yourself
systems.best_for: Running huge MoE models (DeepSeek-V3/R1-class, 600B+ params) on a single workstation by offloading experts to CPU RAM instead of needing enough GPU VRAM to hold the whole model
systems.watch: Billed by its own maintainers as a 'research project'; its headline throughput numbers (e.g. 227.85 tok/s on DeepSeek-R1) were measured on 8x NVIDIA L20 (48GB) GPUs — a serious multi-GPU workstation, not a typical single consumer card, so single-GPU throughput will be markedly lower
systems.standout: CPU-GPU heterogeneous inference purpose-built to run 600B+-parameter MoE models like DeepSeek-R1 on a single workstation instead of a GPU cluster
systems.architecture: Python/C++ with custom CPU+GPU heterogeneous compute kernels
systems.throughput_note: 227.85 tok/s on DeepSeek-R1-0528, measured on 8x NVIDIA L20 GPUs; 3.7 it/s training speed on DeepSeek-V3 with 4x RTX 4090s (project's own reported figures)
systems.verification_note: Confirmed against kvcache-ai/ktransformers GitHub README; throughput figures are the project's own reported benchmark, not independently reproduced

systems.name: WebLLM
systems.price_note: Free, open source, self-hostable (runs entirely client-side, no server inference cost)
systems.model_formats: MLC-compiled model format (same TVM pipeline as MLC LLM); supports Llama/Phi/Gemma/Mistral/Qwen-family models from the MLC model list
systems.hardware_support: Any WebGPU-capable browser; uses WebAssembly for CPU-side execution; no server or native install at all
systems.api_note: Fully OpenAI-API-compatible in-browser client, including streaming, JSON mode, and preliminary function calling
systems.runs_on: Runs entirely inside a web page (or browser extension), typically in a web worker/service worker — no backend process at all
systems.best_for: Shipping a chat feature that runs 100% client-side in the visitor's browser with zero server inference cost and no data leaving their machine
systems.watch: Requires a WebGPU-capable browser — no fallback for browsers/devices without WebGPU, and first-load model download/compile time can be substantial
systems.standout: Runs entirely client-side in a web page via WebGPU — no server, no install, and by construction the model never leaves the visitor's browser
systems.architecture: Apache TVM's WebAssembly runtime (TVMjs) compiled to run in-browser
systems.verification_note: Confirmed against mlc-ai/web-llm GitHub README

systems.name: IPEX-LLM
systems.model_formats: GGUF, AWQ, GPTQ, plus its own INT4/INT2/INT8/FP4/FP6/FP8 and FP16/BF16 quantization support across 70+ verified models
systems.hardware_support: Intel Arc discrete GPUs (Arc, Flex, Max), Intel Core Ultra integrated GPU, Intel Core Ultra NPU (100H/200V/200K/200H series), and Intel CPU
systems.api_note: Not a standalone API server itself — it accelerates llama.cpp, Ollama, HuggingFace, LangChain, LlamaIndex, vLLM, and other tools when run on Intel hardware, so it exposes whichever API that host tool provides
systems.runs_on: A library/acceleration layer plus 'Portable Zip' distributions that bundle Ollama or llama.cpp pre-wired to use it, for Windows/Linux
systems.best_for: Intel Arc GPU or Core Ultra NPU/iGPU owners who want their existing llama.cpp/Ollama workflow to actually use that hardware
systems.watch: Archived by Intel on 2026-01-28 — the repository is now read-only, Intel will not provide further development, support, bug fixes or new releases, and the project's own archive notice states it "has been identified as having known security issues." Existing releases still run, but there is no path to a fix if you hit one.
systems.standout: Lets DeepSeek V3/R1 671B or Qwen3MoE 235B run with just one or two Intel Arc GPUs by accelerating the existing llama.cpp/Ollama/vLLM stack rather than being a separate app
systems.architecture: Python acceleration library built on Intel's XPU/oneAPI stack, integrating into existing inference tools rather than replacing them
systems.verification_note: Archived status (2026-01-28) and the README's own archive notice, including its "known security issues" disclosure, confirmed directly against the current intel/ipex-llm GitHub repository (formerly intel-analytics/ipex-llm — GitHub redirects the old org name) and the GitHub REST API's `archived` field.

systems.name: PocketPal AI
systems.model_formats: GGUF, chosen/downloaded per-device from Hugging Face at a quantization matching the phone's memory
systems.hardware_support: CPU (universal fallback); GPU via Metal on iOS and OpenCL on Qualcomm Adreno for Android; NPU via Qualcomm Hexagon, with graceful fallback and partial layer offload when a full backend isn't available
systems.api_note: Native mobile app only — no documented API server
systems.runs_on: Native iOS and Android apps
systems.best_for: Running a small language model entirely offline on a phone, with no data ever leaving the device
systems.watch: Practical model size is capped hard by phone RAM/storage — this is a small-language-model tool, not a place to run anything near frontier-scale local models
systems.standout: A phone-native app (not a desktop tool ported down) purpose-built for fully offline on-device chat with automatic CPU/GPU/NPU fallback
systems.architecture: React Native mobile app around a llama.cpp-based on-device engine
systems.verification_note: Confirmed against a-ghorbani/pocketpal-ai GitHub repository and the official pocketpal.dev site

systems.name: Text Generation Inference (TGI)
systems.price_note: Free / self-host (open-source; also the engine behind Hugging Face's own paid Inference Endpoints product)
systems.model_formats: Safetensors (HF Transformers architectures) with bitsandbytes and GPT-Q quantization; no native GGUF support.
systems.hardware_support: NVIDIA CUDA (primary), plus AMD ROCm, Intel Gaudi, AWS Inferentia2, and Google TPU via separate hardware-specific images/branches.
systems.api_note: OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions alongside its own native /generate endpoint, with SSE token streaming.
systems.runs_on: Docker container (the officially recommended path) or a pip-installed Rust/Python server process.
systems.best_for: Teams already inside the Hugging Face ecosystem (Inference Endpoints, existing TGI deployments) who want a stable, low-maintenance server rather than the newest throughput ceiling — new deployments should read the maintenance-mode notice first.
systems.watch: As of the project's own README, TGI is in maintenance mode: Hugging Face states it is only accepting minor bug-fix and documentation PRs, and explicitly recommends vLLM or SGLang for new deployments going forward — this is HF's own stated position, not third-party speculation.
systems.standout: The engine that popularized continuous batching plus Paged Attention for the wider ecosystem before Hugging Face itself began redirecting new users elsewhere; still the deployment path underlying HF's own Inference Endpoints product.
systems.architecture: Continuous batching with Flash Attention and Paged Attention (adopted from vLLM) on supported architectures; Tensor Parallelism for multi-GPU.
systems.streaming: Yes — token streaming via Server-Sent Events.
systems.released: 2022 (initial release); briefly relicensed HFOIL 1.0 in mid-2023, reverted to Apache-2.0 in April 2024 (v2.0.0); now in maintenance mode
systems.verification_note: Licence history confirmed via github.com/huggingface/text-generation-inference (LICENSE file + issue #726 + the v2.0.0 revert commit). Maintenance-mode notice quoted from the repository's own current README.

systems.name: LMDeploy
systems.model_formats: HuggingFace safetensors converted into LMDeploy's own TurboMind engine format (or run directly via its pure-Python PyTorch engine); AWQ/GPTQ 4-bit weight quantization plus online INT4/INT8 KV-cache quantization; no GGUF support.
systems.hardware_support: NVIDIA CUDA (primary; prebuilt wheels target CUDA 12.8 / RTX 50-series); community-maintained builds also target Huawei Ascend, AMD ROCm, MetaX (MACA), and Cambricon NPUs.
systems.api_note: OpenAI-compatible API server (`lmdeploy serve api_server`), with a proxy layer for distributing requests across multiple machines/GPUs.
systems.runs_on: pip-installed Python package or Docker container.
systems.best_for: Serving InternLM/Qwen-family and other checkpoints with a specific, checkable throughput edge over vLLM, when NVIDIA CUDA is the target hardware.
systems.watch: TurboMind is the fast path but converts weights into its own internal engine format on load; the pure-Python PyTorch engine is the fallback for architectures TurboMind hasn't implemented yet, at lower throughput.
systems.standout: Publishes a specific, checkable throughput claim (up to 1.8x vLLM request throughput) tied to its persistent-batch TurboMind engine, rather than a vaguer marketing number.
systems.architecture: TurboMind's "persistent batch" (its term for continuous batching) with a blocked/paged KV-cache manager and dynamic split-and-fuse scheduling.
systems.throughput_note: Claims up to 1.8x higher request throughput than vLLM via persistent batching, and 16+ RPS on internlm2-20b in its own published figures.
systems.multi_gpu: Yes — tensor-parallel inference, plus multi-machine/multi-card serving via its proxy layer.
systems.streaming: Yes — SSE streaming via its OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
systems.benchmarks: LMDeploy's own project documentation: up to 1.8x higher request throughput than vLLM via persistent batching and blocked KV-cache; 4-bit (AWQ) inference measured at 2.4x FP16 throughput; 16+ RPS achieved serving internlm2-20b with TurboMind.
systems.released: 2023 (initial release, InternLM/Shanghai AI Lab); actively developed
systems.verification_note: Licence and throughput figures read off github.com/InternLM/lmdeploy's README and docs (TurboMind architecture page).

systems.name: Ray Serve LLM
systems.variants: Formerly a standalone project called RayLLM (github.com/ray-project/ray-llm), now archived; today `ray.serve.llm` ships as a module inside the main Ray repository.
systems.price_note: Free / self-host (open-source; Anyscale also sells a managed Ray platform with LLM-serving templates)
systems.model_formats: Whatever its selected backend engine loads — vLLM or SGLang as of the documentation reviewed — so its own format gate is exactly that engine's (safetensors; FP8/AWQ/GPTQ; no native GGUF).
systems.hardware_support: Whatever its underlying engine (vLLM/SGLang) supports on the compute side, orchestrated across a Ray cluster for multi-node deployments.
systems.api_note: OpenAI-compatible REST API, confirmed in Ray's own docs, usable directly with the OpenAI Python SDK.
systems.runs_on: Python library (`ray.serve.llm`) deployed onto a Ray cluster via `pip install ray[serve,llm]`; not a standalone server binary.
systems.best_for: Teams already running Ray for other ML workloads who want LLM serving with autoscaling and scale-to-zero in the same Python-native deployment story, rather than a from-scratch new stack.
systems.watch: The earlier standalone ray-project/ray-llm ("RayLLM") repository is archived and no longer maintained; the current implementation lives inside the main Ray repo as the ray.serve.llm module — citing the old repo name points at dead code.
systems.standout: The only row here whose main selling point is autoscaling behavior (including scale-to-zero) rather than raw per-GPU throughput — it answers "how do I run this at variable load in production," not "how many tokens/sec."
systems.architecture: Delegates batching/KV-cache strategy entirely to its selected backend engine (vLLM or SGLang); Ray Serve's own contribution is autoscaling, request routing, and multi-node placement above that, including prefill-decode disaggregation support.
systems.multi_gpu: Yes — multi-node deployments with automatic placement, including models that span more nodes than fit on one.
systems.streaming: Yes — SSE streaming via its OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
systems.released: Ray Serve since ~2021; ray.serve.llm APIs added and folded into the main Ray repo 2024–2025
systems.verification_note: Licence and current-repo location confirmed via docs.ray.io/en/latest/serve/llm and github.com/ray-project/ray-llm's own archived-notice README.

systems.name: OpenLLM
systems.price_note: Free / self-host (also deployable to BentoML's paid BentoCloud platform)
systems.model_formats: Safetensors via its vLLM production backend — the same format gate as vLLM itself; custom model repositories also supported.
systems.hardware_support: Whatever its vLLM backend supports (NVIDIA CUDA primarily); the project's own deployment examples range from a single 12GB GPU (Gemma2) up to 16x80GB GPUs (DeepSeek R1-671B).
systems.api_note: OpenAI-compatible APIs for chat/completions, plus a built-in web chat UI at /chat.
systems.runs_on: Docker container, a BentoML-packaged "Bento," or deployed to BentoCloud; also runnable via a single CLI command locally.
systems.best_for: Teams that want vLLM's throughput with a one-command deploy story and an optional path to BentoCloud's managed hosting, without operating vLLM's own CLI/config surface directly.
systems.watch: Runs on vLLM as its production backend, so it inherits vLLM's own format gate and hardware requirements rather than adding a distinct one — it is not an alternative inference kernel.
systems.standout: Thinnest layer in this matrix by design — a one-command wrapper that hands the actual serving work to vLLM, aimed at teams who want vLLM's throughput without hand-rolling the deployment plumbing.
systems.architecture: Inherits vLLM's PagedAttention/continuous-batching architecture via its vLLM backend; OpenLLM's own layer is packaging and deployment, not a distinct scheduler.
systems.multi_gpu: Yes, inherited from its vLLM backend.
systems.streaming: Yes — SSE streaming via its OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
systems.verification_note: Licence and vLLM-backend dependency read off github.com/bentoml/OpenLLM's README.

systems.name: Mooncake
systems.model_formats: Not a model-loading engine at all — Transfer Engine and Mooncake Store move and cache KV-cache tensors and model weights across nodes for vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, LMDeploy, and vLLM-Ascend; the format gate is whichever of those it's paired with.
systems.hardware_support: NVIDIA, AMD, Huawei Ascend, Cambricon, and AWS infrastructure, via CUDA/HIP/MUSA/RDMA/NVMe-oF transport backends — this is the KV-cache transfer layer, not model compute itself.
systems.api_note: None of its own — Mooncake is a transfer/cache layer with no user-facing inference API; the OpenAI-compatible endpoint is whichever engine (vLLM, SGLang, etc.) it's paired with.
systems.runs_on: A set of libraries/services (Transfer Engine, Mooncake Store) deployed alongside an inference engine's own process — not a standalone server on its own.
systems.best_for: High-QPS production services (like Moonshot's own Kimi) that need to pool and reuse KV-cache across a prefill/decode-disaggregated cluster rather than recomputing or discarding it per request.
systems.watch: Not an inference engine — it's a KV-cache transfer/storage layer that plugs into vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, LMDeploy, or vLLM-Ascend; choosing Mooncake is an infrastructure decision layered on top of one of those engines, not an alternative to them.
systems.standout: Won a Best Paper Award at FAST 2025 for its KVCache-centric disaggregated architecture, and is the system actually running Moonshot AI's production Kimi service, not just a research prototype.
systems.architecture: KVCache-centric disaggregated architecture: separate prefill/decode clusters sharing a pooled, tiered (DRAM/SSD/RDMA-networked) KV-cache managed by a dedicated scheduler.
systems.multi_gpu: N/A directly — it moves/pools KV-cache across whatever multi-GPU/multi-node cluster an engine like vLLM or SGLang is already running on.
systems.benchmarks: Mooncake's own published figures: Transfer Engine moves 40GB (equivalent to 128k tokens in LLaMA3-70B) at up to 87 GB/s over a 4x200 Gbps network and 190 GB/s over 8x400 Gbps (2.4x/4.6x faster than TCP); up to 525% throughput increase in the project's simulated SLO scenarios; enables Moonshot AI's Kimi service to handle 75% more requests under real production workloads.
systems.released: Paper published June 2024 (arXiv 2407.00079); Transfer Engine open-sourced November 2024; Mooncake Store open-sourced March 2025
systems.verification_note: Licence (Apache-2.0) and figures read off github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake's README and its FAST 2025 paper; production use confirmed as Moonshot AI's own stated deployment of Mooncake for Kimi.

systems.name: TensorRT-LLM
systems.licence: Apache License 2.0 (core code), but the repo bundles a separate non-open "LTX-2 Community License Agreement" (restricted-use terms covering the LTX-2 visual-generation model integration), which is why GitHub's own license detector classifies the repository as "Other" (spdx_id: NOASSERTION) rather than a clean Apache-2.0
systems.price_note: Free and self-hosted (Apache-2.0 core); no NVIDIA-hosted paid serving tier -- the only cost is the NVIDIA GPU hardware or cloud instance you run it on
systems.model_formats: Current default (since v1.0, confirmed still default in the current stable v1.2.1 and on the main branch docs): PyTorch-native backend. trtllm-serve loads a raw Hugging Face model id or local checkpoint directory directly (e.g. trtllm-serve "TinyLlama/TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0") -- no separate build/compile step. Pre-quantized NVIDIA Model Optimizer (ModelOpt) checkpoints also load directly this way. Legacy opt-in path (still present and functional in the current stable release v1.2.1, selected with --backend trt): the original ahead-of-time (AOT) flow that compiles an HF/NeMo checkpoint into a TensorRT .engine/.plan file via the trtllm-build CLI before serving. The project's unreleased main-branch release notes (heading toward v1.3.0, currently in RC) document a breaking change that fully removes the TensorRT backend, trtllm-build, trtllm-refit, trtllm-prune, and --backend tensorrt, making PyTorch the sole backend. That removal had NOT shipped in a stable release as of Aug 2026.
systems.hardware_support: NVIDIA CUDA GPUs only -- no ROCm/AMD GPU support and no CPU-only inference path found in the docs. Per the project's Supported Hardware page and release notes, officially validated generations are distinct: NVIDIA Ampere (SM80, SM86), NVIDIA Ada Lovelace (SM89), NVIDIA Hopper (SM90), and NVIDIA Blackwell (SM100/SM103, SM120). Per the quantization support matrix: FP8 requires Ada Lovelace (SM89) or newer; NVFP4/MXFP4 require Blackwell; Ampere lacks FP8 support entirely.
systems.api_note: Built-in OpenAI-compatible HTTP server via trtllm-serve: /v1/completions, /v1/chat/completions, /v1/models, plus a trtllm-serve embeddings subcommand exposing /v1/embeddings. Utility endpoints: /health, /metrics, /version. Also ships a native Python LLM API for in-process/offline inference, and integrates with NVIDIA Triton Inference Server and NVIDIA Dynamo.
systems.runs_on: Self-hosted only. Install via pip install tensorrt_llm or pre-built NGC Docker release containers. Deploy via the trtllm-serve OpenAI-compatible server (default PyTorch backend, direct HF load, no build step) or, opt-in, via the legacy AOT trtllm-build to .engine flow with --backend trt (still present in the current stable release, slated for removal in the next major version). No hosted/managed SaaS offering from NVIDIA.
systems.best_for: Squeezing maximum throughput/latency out of NVIDIA datacenter GPUs (Ampere and newer) for production LLM serving at scale -- especially teams already standardized on NVIDIA hardware who want native FP8/FP4/AWQ/GPTQ quantization and an OpenAI-compatible server without leaving the CUDA ecosystem.
systems.watch: The legacy AOT --backend trt / trtllm-build path (still shipping in the current stable release) is being fully removed in the next major release per the project's own migration guide -- anything built around that workflow needs a migration plan to the PyTorch backend. Separately, the repo's license is not a clean Apache-2.0: it bundles the restrictive "LTX-2 Community License Agreement," which is why GitHub flags the whole repo as "Other."
systems.standout: PyTorch-native architecture with day-0 support for the latest model releases and vendor-claimed state-of-the-art throughput on NVIDIA's newest Blackwell GPUs.
systems.architecture: PyTorch-native ("Architected on PyTorch") high-level Python LLM API on top of custom CUDA kernels (CUTLASS, FlashInfer, in-house kernels) and NVIDIA TensorRT; includes in-flight batching, paged KV cache with block reuse, chunked prefill/attention, and pluggable speculative decoding.
systems.throughput_note: Vendor-claimed (NVIDIA blog posts, not independently reproduced here): "world-record" DeepSeek R1 inference performance on Blackwell GPUs. Independently, in MLPerf Inference v6.0 (April 2026) TensorRT-LLM served as one of NVIDIA's baseline engines alongside vLLM/SGLang.
systems.multi_gpu: Tensor Parallel, Pipeline Parallel, Data Parallel, Expert Parallel, Context Parallel, and Wide Expert Parallel (for large MoE models), configurable both offline and at serve time, across single or multiple nodes.
systems.streaming: Streaming responses over the OpenAI-compatible chat/completions endpoints.
systems.context_note: Chunked context/prefill decouples per-iteration memory use from raw input length; there is no single engine-wide context limit -- effective max context is model- and memory-dependent.
systems.quantisation: FP4 (NVFP4) and MXFP4; FP8 (per-tensor, block-scaling, rowwise, and FP8/NVFP4 KV cache); INT4/INT8 AWQ (W4A16, W4A8); INT4/INT8 GPTQ (W4A16, W4A8). Runs pre-quantized checkpoints from the NVIDIA Model Optimizer (ModelOpt) Hugging Face collection directly. No GGUF or EXL2 support found.
systems.benchmarks: MLPerf Inference v6.0 (April 2026), per a third-party (Lambda) write-up of an NVIDIA submission: an 8x NVIDIA HGX B200 system running TensorRT-LLM measured 130,008 tok/s (Server scenario) on Llama 3.1 8B. This is a third-party blog's recounting of official MLPerf figures, not a direct read of the MLCommons results table.
systems.adoption: 14.3k GitHub stars / 2.6k forks as of Aug 2026, actively pushed to within the last day. Used as one of NVIDIA's baseline/reference serving engines in MLPerf Inference v6.0 (April 2026).
systems.released: GitHub repo's initial commit is dated 2023-09-20; first tagged release v0.5.0 shipped 2023-10-19. Latest stable release as of Aug 2026 is v1.2.1.
systems.verification_note: Verified directly against primary sources: raw GitHub source files on the main branch (docs, release notes) and the GitHub REST API (repo metadata, license detection, commit history). Confirmed the initial commit is 2023-09-20 and no relicensing occurred since -- the earlier 'relicensed Apache 2.0 in September 2024' claim is false and not repeated. Confirmed trtllm-build/trtllm-prune/trtllm-refit are still registered console scripts at the current stable tag, while the full removal of that path is documented only on the unreleased main branch. The throughput_note and adoption/benchmarks rely on NVIDIA vendor blog claims and a secondary blog's recounting of MLPerf figures rather than the primary MLCommons results table itself, hence the overall 'mixed' rating.

systems.name: ExLlamaV3
systems.model_formats: EXL3 — the project's own format, a streamlined variant of Cornell RelaxML's QTIP trellis-coded quantization
systems.hardware_support: NVIDIA CUDA 12.4+ GPUs; ROCm/AMD support is listed on the project's to-do list, not yet shipped
systems.api_note: Ships a Python library (e.g. chat.py example, dynamic generator) with no bundled server of its own. The official/recommended server is TabbyAPI, providing an OpenAI-compatible API plus HF model downloading.
systems.runs_on: Self-hosted only (local GPU)
systems.best_for: Getting usable coherence at extreme low bitrates (down to ~1.6bpw) via trellis-coded quantization on a single modern NVIDIA GPU — more accuracy per bit than EXL2/GPTQ/AWQ at the same size.
systems.watch: EXL3 conversion is meaningfully slower than EXL2/GPTQ to produce (minutes to hours per model on one GPU), and AMD/ROCm is not yet supported — NVIDIA-only today.
systems.standout: Lower coherent bitrate than any other mainstream local format (~1.6bpw stays usable) by using QTIP-style trellis coding instead of per-channel scale/zero-point quantization.
systems.architecture: Python + custom CUDA kernels implementing QTIP-derived tail-biting trellis codebooks; tensor-parallel and expert-parallel inference paths for consumer multi-GPU setups
systems.multi_gpu: Yes — tensor-parallel and expert-parallel inference support for consumer hardware
systems.streaming: Yes, via the generator API and TabbyAPI's OpenAI-compatible streaming
systems.quantisation: EXL3: variable bitrate down to ~1.6bpw via QTIP-style trellis codebooks; conversion needs only an input HF model and a target bitrate
systems.free_tier: N/A — entire project is free and open source
systems.tunables: Target bitrate at conversion time, tensor/expert-parallel split, KV cache quantization
systems.adoption: ~1.1k GitHub stars at time of research; the direct, currently-developed successor to ExLlamaV2 and the author's primary focus going forward.
systems.released: Actively developed as the successor to ExLlamaV2
systems.verification_note: Format lineage (streamlined QTIP variant), CUDA 12.4+ requirement, 16GB/70B/1.6bpw claim, and TabbyAPI as official server read directly from the official turboderp-org/exllamav3 GitHub README and its doc/exl3.md page.

systems.name: AutoGPTQ
systems.model_formats: GPTQ — 4-bit (and lower) post-training weight quantization; this project's checkpoint layout became the de facto community GPTQ standard
systems.hardware_support: NVIDIA CUDA (11.8/12.1) and AMD ROCm 5.7 GPUs on Linux/Windows; Intel Gaudi 2 HPU support; explicitly does not support pre-Turing (Maxwell or older) NVIDIA cards
systems.api_note: Own AutoGPTQForCausalLM class with a Hugging Face-compatible .generate()/pipeline API; can plug in ExLlamaV2 or Marlin kernels as faster optional inference backends
systems.runs_on: Self-hosted only
systems.best_for: Historical reference / already-deployed legacy stacks — for any new GPTQ work the project's own README now points to GPTQModel.
systems.watch: Repository is archived and its own README states: "AutoGPTQ is unmaintained — we suggest using GPTQModel for bug fixes and new models support." Do not start new work on it.
systems.standout: n/a — superseded by GPTQModel
systems.architecture: PyTorch + CUDA/Triton kernels; became the reference GPTQ implementation integrated into Hugging Face Transformers, Optimum and PEFT during its active years
systems.quantisation: GPTQ, primarily 4-bit, with 2/3-bit options (3-bit unsupported on the Triton backend)
systems.fine_tuning: LoRA/PEFT fine-tuning of GPTQ-quantized models was supported
systems.adoption: Was the reference GPTQ implementation, integrated natively into Hugging Face Transformers/Optimum/PEFT — likely the most widely deployed GPTQ engine of 2023-2024.
systems.verification_note: Archived status and the "unmaintained, use GPTQModel" notice, license, and hardware matrix read directly from the official AutoGPTQ/AutoGPTQ GitHub README.

systems.name: GPTQModel
systems.licence: Apache-2.0 core; one optional performance kernel ("Swordfish", for Blackwell GPUs) is AGPL-3.0-or-later and is only JIT-compiled/linked at runtime if enabled
systems.model_formats: GPTQ (its origin and still primary/native format); has since added native quantize/inference paths for GGUF, FP8, EXL3 and its own ParoQuant, alongside AWQ, QQQ, GPTAQ and FOEM
systems.hardware_support: NVIDIA CUDA (Turing/sm_75+, including Blackwell), AMD ROCm 6.2+ (7900XT+), Intel XPU (Arc, Datacenter Max) and CPU (AVX2/AVX512/AMX), Huawei Ascend NPU (via torch-npu), Apple Metal GPU and M1+ CPU — Linux/macOS/Windows
systems.api_note: Own Python API (GPTQModel.load(...).generate(...)), plus native integration as a quantization/inference backend inside Hugging Face Transformers, vLLM (dynamic batching) and SGLang (optimized serving). Its own README notes vLLM/SGLang integration currently targets only GPTQ and AWQ, not the newer formats it can also produce.
systems.runs_on: Self-hosted only
systems.best_for: Teams standardized on GPTQ who want the currently-maintained toolkit — the direct successor to AutoGPTQ and AutoAWQ, with the widest hardware matrix of any GPTQ-lineage tool (adds AMD, Intel, Ascend NPU and Apple Silicon).
systems.watch: Its own README states GPTQ and AWQ remain the only formats vLLM/SGLang actually integrate today — the newer native formats (GGUF/FP8/EXL3/ParoQuant) it can quantize to are not yet backed by the same serving-side integration, so confirm your serving target before picking a format. Also weigh the optional AGPL-3.0 Swordfish kernel if your project needs permissive-only dependencies.
systems.standout: Widest hardware matrix of any GPTQ-format engine (AutoGPTQ was NVIDIA/AMD/Gaudi-only) and the only actively maintained option in the GPTQ lineage — though it is visibly drifting from single-format toward a broader toolkit.
systems.architecture: PyTorch + CUDA/Triton/ROCm/XPU kernels, with JIT-compiled optional kernels including the AGPL-licensed Swordfish kernel for Blackwell
systems.multi_gpu: Yes — multi-GPU data-parallel quantization (project claims 80%+ faster for MoE models)
systems.quantisation: GPTQ (primary), plus AWQ/QQQ/GPTAQ/FOEM/ParoQuant/GGUF/FP8/EXL3 as the toolkit has broadened; per-module dynamic quantization control; MoE expert-routing overrides
systems.tunables: Per-module bit-width overrides, MoE expert bypass/override/failsafe routing, quantization method selection
systems.verification_note: License split, format list, hardware matrix and "supersedes AutoGPTQ/AutoAWQ" claim read directly from the official ModelCloud/GPTQModel GitHub README.

systems.name: bitnet.cpp
systems.model_formats: BitNet b1.58 ternary weights (~1.58 bits/weight) packed in a GGUF variant (e.g. ggml-model-i2_s.gguf); two kernel schemes, I2_S and TL1
systems.hardware_support: CPU: x86 (AVX2) and ARM (NEON); GPU inference kernels also shipped (added May 2025); NPU support listed as "coming next"
systems.api_note: CLI inference (run_inference.py), a bundled inference server script (run_inference_server.py) for API-based deployment, and an e2e_benchmark.py benchmarking harness
systems.runs_on: Self-hosted only (CPU-first, GPU optional)
systems.best_for: Running natively ternary-trained BitNet b1.58 models — not arbitrary existing LLMs — at genuinely fast CPU-only speeds; the project's own claim is 5-7 tok/s for a 100B-parameter model on a single CPU.
systems.watch: This is not a general quantizer — you cannot point it at an arbitrary fp16 checkpoint. It only runs models pretrained or fine-tuned with BitNet's quantization-aware-training recipe, which today is a small model catalog (chiefly Microsoft's own BitNet b1.58 releases and a handful of community conversions).
systems.standout: The only mainstream engine here built around native ternary (1-bit-class) training rather than post-training compression of an existing fp16 model; its CPU-only throughput claims are the strongest in this matrix for a compatible model.
systems.architecture: Built on llama.cpp/ggml infrastructure, using lookup-table (LUT) kernel methodology pioneered by Microsoft's own T-MAC project
systems.quantisation: Fixed at ternary (~1.58 bits/weight) — this is NOT a post-training compressor for arbitrary checkpoints; models must be pretrained or fine-tuned natively in BitNet's quantization-aware-training scheme before bitnet.cpp can run them
systems.tunables: Kernel scheme selection (I2_S vs TL1), CPU thread count
systems.benchmarks: Vendor-reported (project README): 2.37x-6.17x speedup on x86, 1.37x-5.07x on ARM, with 71.9%-82.2% (x86) / 55.4%-70.0% (ARM) energy reduction vs. an unstated baseline
systems.adoption: Official Microsoft Research framework for the BitNet line, with updates continuing into mid-2026; the standard runtime for the small catalog of models trained natively in the ternary BitNet b1.58 scheme.
systems.released: v1.0 released October 17, 2024; GPU kernels added May 2025; embedding-model support added per the project's July 2026 changelog entry
systems.verification_note: Format, kernels, hardware and throughput claims read directly from the official microsoft/BitNet GitHub README. The "must be natively trained ternary" constraint is corroborated by BitNet's own arXiv technical report (arxiv.org/abs/2504.12285) describing quantization-aware training vs. post-training quantization.

systems.name: VPTQ
systems.model_formats: VPTQ — Vector Post-Training Quantization, extreme low-bit (roughly 1.375-4 bits/weight) via vector-quantization codebooks
systems.hardware_support: NVIDIA CUDA (primary); early/preliminary AMD ROCm support noted
systems.api_note: Own CLI (python -m vptq --model=<name> --prompt=...), a chat mode (--chat), and a Gradio web app (python -m vptq.app); also integrated into Hugging Face Transformers (since v4.48.0) and, as of Feb 2025, into Aphrodite Engine as the first third-party serving engine to add VPTQ support
systems.runs_on: Self-hosted only (local GPU or Google Colab)
systems.best_for: Extreme compression of very large models (70B-405B class) down to 1-2 bits/weight for single- or few-GPU inference, when a multi-hour-plus quantization cost is acceptable for the memory win.
systems.watch: Quantizing a large model is a serious time cost, not a quick pass — the project reports ~17 hours to quantize a 405B Llama-3.1 model on its own hardware — and vLLM/llama.cpp/ExLlama integration remains on the roadmap, not shipped, so today it only runs via VPTQ's own CLI/chat/web app, Hugging Face Transformers, or Aphrodite Engine.
systems.standout: One of the only formats in this matrix that ships its own runnable CLI/chat/web-app out of the box, rather than requiring you to wire it into a separate serving stack yourself.
systems.architecture: Second-order-optimization-guided vector quantization with a Python/CUDA runtime
systems.quantisation: 1.375 to ~4 bits/weight via learned vector codebooks; project reports ~17 hours to quantize a 405B Llama-3.1 model on its hardware
systems.adoption: Adopted into Hugging Face Transformers as a supported quantization method (Dec 2024) and picked up by Aphrodite Engine (Feb 2025) as its first third-party inference-engine integration; vLLM/llama.cpp/ExLlama integration is listed on the project's roadmap but not shipped.
systems.released: PyPI v0.0.5, January 18 2025; DeepSeek R1 inference support added March 2025
systems.verification_note: CLI/chat/Gradio inference commands, Transformers integration date and Aphrodite-engine adoption read directly from the official microsoft/VPTQ GitHub README; could not confirm project activity beyond March 2025 in the sources reviewed, flagged above rather than assumed current.

systems.name: QTIP
systems.model_formats: QTIP — trellis-coded quantization (bitshift trellis + incoherence processing), 2/3/4-bit
systems.hardware_support: NVIDIA GPUs (benchmarked on RTX 6000 Ada); built on the QuIP# CUDA kernel codebase
systems.api_note: Ships eval/interactive_gen.py (python -m eval.interactive_gen --hf_path ... --streaming), a streaming-capable reference generation script with CUDA-graph support — again a reference script rather than a bundled production server
systems.runs_on: Self-hosted only
systems.best_for: The current state of the art in this lattice/trellis lineage — same inference throughput as QuIP# with better quantization quality — for teams willing to run a research-grade rather than turnkey-production engine.
systems.watch: Ships as a research-grade reference implementation rather than a turnkey production server — eval/interactive_gen.py is a reference generation script (with CUDA-graph support), so wiring it into an actual serving stack is left to the user. Also note the GPL-3.0 licence (copyleft), which differs from the permissive MIT/Apache terms most of this matrix uses.
systems.standout: Best quantization-quality-per-bit in the trellis/lattice family reviewed here, achieved without sacrificing QuIP#'s inference speed, per the authors' own comparison.
systems.architecture: PyTorch + custom CUDA kernels; a fork/evolution of the QuIP# codebase adding a hardware-efficient bitshift trellis and compute-based random Gaussian codes so no trellis structure or codebook needs to be stored at decode time
systems.quantisation: 2, 3 and 4 bits/weight via bitshift-trellis coded quantization
systems.adoption: Direct, currently-maintained successor to QuIP# from Cornell RelaxML, with a pre-quantized model collection published on Hugging Face.
systems.released: Paper released June 2024 (arXiv 2406.11235); repository still updated, with the same lab's newer YAQA rounding algorithm referenced as a compatible drop-in improvement
systems.verification_note: Format description, interactive_gen.py usage, GPLv3 license and QuIP# lineage read directly from the official Cornell-RelaxML/qtip GitHub README.

systems.name: QServe (OmniServe)
systems.model_formats: QoQ — "quattuor-octo-quattuor" W4A8KV4 (4-bit weights, 8-bit activations, 4-bit KV cache), with W4A8KV8/W8A8KV4/W8A8KV8 variants also selectable
systems.hardware_support: NVIDIA GPUs only — benchmarked on A100 (recommended for per-channel QServe) and L40S (recommended for per-group QServe); no AMD/Intel support documented
systems.api_note: A research serving system with its own benchmark/serving harness built for direct throughput comparison against TensorRT-LLM; the README as reviewed does not document a bundled OpenAI-compatible HTTP API the way TabbyAPI does for ExLlama
systems.runs_on: Self-hosted only
systems.best_for: Squeezing maximum GPU serving throughput out of a quantization scheme co-designed for the serving pipeline itself — the project's headline claim is beating TensorRT-LLM's throughput at equivalent quality.
systems.watch: Closer to a research serving system than a turnkey deployment tool — no documented OpenAI-compatible API layer, NVIDIA-only, and activity beyond the Feb 2025 unification announcement was not confirmed in the sources reviewed. Verify current maintenance status before depending on it.
systems.standout: The only entry in this matrix where the quantization format (QoQ) and the serving engine were co-designed together specifically to beat a production serving baseline (TensorRT-LLM) on throughput, rather than being a weight-compression method retrofitted onto generic serving.
systems.architecture: Compute-aware weight reordering, register-level-parallel dequantization, and a fused memory-bound attention kernel co-designed with the QoQ algorithm; unifies MLSys'25 QServe (quantization/serving) with the same lab's LServe (long-context sparse attention) into one framework
systems.throughput_note: Vendor-reported (MLSys'25 paper + README): 1.2x-1.4x higher throughput than TensorRT-LLM serving Llama-3-8B, 2.4x-3.5x higher serving Qwen1.5-72B, on L40S/A100 GPUs
systems.quantisation: W4A8KV4 (QoQ) as the headline scheme, with W4A8KV8/W8A8KV4/W8A8KV8 alternatives
systems.released: Public February 2025 (QServe + LServe merged into the OmniServe framework); both accepted at MLSys 2025
systems.verification_note: Format, hardware recommendations, throughput claims and the Feb 2025 QServe+LServe unification read directly from the official mit-han-lab/omniserve GitHub README; throughput multipliers are the project's own self-reported benchmark, not independently reproduced by this research.

systems.name: MLC-LLM (MLCEngine)
systems.model_formats: Compiles Hugging Face PyTorch/safetensors checkpoints via the TVM Unity compiler into a target-specific compiled artifact (shared library, WASM, or app binary) per device
systems.hardware_support: Generates kernels per target: CUDA, Metal, Vulkan, ROCm, OpenCL, WebGPU; CPU via LLVM (ARM/x86)
systems.api_note: MLCEngine exposes an OpenAI-compatible REST server plus Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, iOS, and Android SDKs
systems.runs_on: Any device the TVM Unity compiler targets — phones (iOS/Android), browsers (WebGPU), desktop/server GPUs
systems.best_for: Deploying one model across many device types by ahead-of-time compiling a dedicated artifact for each, rather than shipping one generic runtime
systems.watch: Not a single cross-platform binary: each target (CUDA/Metal/Vulkan/WebGPU/iOS/Android) needs its own compiled artifact, so adding a new device means a new build.
systems.verification_note: License confirmed from repo LICENSE file (Apache-2.0); project active since at least mid-2023 per Internet Archive snapshots, exact founding date not published.

systems.name: AWS Neuron SDK
systems.licence: Mixed — Neuron compiler/runtime under a custom AWS SDK license; framework integrations (transformers-neuronx, NxD Inference, vLLM plugin) are separately open-sourced
systems.price_note: SDK is free; billed through AWS EC2 Inf2/Trn1/Trn2 instance hourly pricing
systems.model_formats: Loads Hugging Face PyTorch/safetensors checkpoints; compiles via the Neuron Compiler (neuronx-cc) to NEFF artifacts
systems.hardware_support: AWS Inferentia (Inf1/Inf2) and Trainium (Trn1/Trn2) accelerators only
systems.api_note: NxD Inference integrates as a vLLM plugin/backend, giving an OpenAI-compatible server; also exposes raw PyTorch/XLA APIs
systems.runs_on: AWS EC2 Inf/Trn instances or SageMaker — cloud only
systems.best_for: Teams already on AWS wanting lower cost-per-token than GPU instances by using Amazon's own inference/training accelerators
systems.watch: SDK only works inside AWS EC2/SageMaker on Inf/Trn instances — Amazon does not sell Inferentia/Trainium chips for on-prem deployment.
systems.verification_note: vLLM/NxD Inference integration confirmed via AWS's own 'what's new' post and Neuron/vLLM official docs.

systems.name: Qualcomm AI Engine Direct / Genie (QAIRT)
systems.licence: Proprietary Qualcomm SDK license (QAIRT/QNN); community GenieX layer is BSD-3-Clause
systems.price_note: Free to download after accepting Qualcomm's SDK license; no runtime fee
systems.model_formats: Exports/quantizes via Qualcomm AI Hub from Hugging Face/PyTorch/ONNX into Genie 'bundle' QNN context-binary format
systems.hardware_support: Qualcomm Snapdragon SoCs only — Hexagon NPU, Adreno GPU, Kryo CPU; mobile (Snapdragon 8 Elite/8 Elite Gen 5) and Windows-on-Snapdragon (X Elite/X2 Elite) laptop chips
systems.api_note: `genie-t2t-run` CLI plus a C++ runtime API; no bundled server by default, though the GenieX community layer targets easier local inference
systems.runs_on: Android phones and Windows-on-Snapdragon PCs with a Qualcomm NPU
systems.best_for: On-device LLM inference on Snapdragon phones and Copilot+ PCs where NPU offload is needed for battery life
systems.watch: Llama-family models require gated Hugging Face access and must be exported yourself via qai-hub-models — no pre-compiled asset is distributed for them.
systems.verification_note: GenieX BSD-3-Clause license confirmed via github.com/qualcomm/geniex; QAIRT/Genie proprietary SDK nature confirmed via Qualcomm docs.qualcomm.com Genie page. source_url independently verified against Qualcomm's own developer page (qualcomm.com/developer/software/gen-ai-inference-extensions), which names Genie, the Neural Processing SDK and the AI Engine Direct SDK together as the one SDK download (the page itself does not use the string "QAIRT").

systems.name: AMD Ryzen AI Software (+ Lemonade SDK)
systems.licence: Mixed — Lemonade SDK and RyzenAI-SW example/doc repos are permissively licensed; NPU driver and Vitis AI/Quark compiler components require accepting a separate AMD EULA
systems.price_note: Free download (EULA click-through for driver/compiler pieces); bundled with AMD Ryzen AI hardware
systems.model_formats: ONNX via ONNX Runtime + Vitis AI/NPU execution provider; Lemonade also loads GGUF for a llama.cpp-backed path
systems.hardware_support: AMD Ryzen AI NPU (XDNA/XDNA2) plus integrated Radeon GPU — Ryzen AI-branded chips only
systems.api_note: Lemonade SDK exposes an OpenAI-compatible server (`lemonade-server`) and a Python API; GAIA layers a local agent UI on top
systems.runs_on: Windows PCs with an AMD Ryzen AI (NPU-equipped) processor; Linux NPU driver support is still maturing
systems.best_for: Offloading LLM inference to the on-chip NPU on Ryzen AI laptops to save battery/thermal budget versus CPU or iGPU execution
systems.watch: Doc/example repos are MIT-licensed, but the NPU driver installer and Vitis AI/Quark compiler binaries require accepting a separate AMD End User License Agreement at install time.
systems.verification_note: EULA requirement confirmed via ryzenai.docs.amd.com/licenses.html and AMD's account.amd.com Ryzen AI EULA acceptance page; Lemonade SDK open-source nature confirmed via AMD developer articles.

systems.name: Tenstorrent TT-Metalium / tt-inference-server
systems.price_note: Free, open source; Tenstorrent accelerator hardware (n150/n300/Galaxy) purchased separately
systems.model_formats: Loads Hugging Face PyTorch checkpoints; TT-NN op library and TT-Forge MLIR compiler produce Tenstorrent-native kernels
systems.hardware_support: Tenstorrent Wormhole/Blackhole accelerators only (n150/n300 PCIe cards, Galaxy/QuietBox systems)
systems.api_note: tt-inference-server wraps models behind a vLLM-compatible OpenAI API; TT-Metalium itself is a lower-level kernel-programming API
systems.runs_on: Servers/workstations with a Tenstorrent PCIe accelerator card
systems.best_for: Teams on owned Tenstorrent hardware wanting a fully open, Apache-2.0 compiler stack down to the kernel level, unlike most vendor NPU SDKs
systems.watch: Requires owning Tenstorrent hardware (Wormhole/Blackhole n150/n300 PCIe cards, or Galaxy/QuietBox systems, purchased separately) — unlike most of this matrix there is no path to running it on NVIDIA/AMD/Intel GPUs.
systems.verification_note: Apache-2.0 license confirmed via repo LICENSE/NOTICE files; tt-inference-server and TT-Forge role confirmed via Tenstorrent's own GitHub org descriptions.

systems.name: Cerebras software stack (CS-3 / Wafer-Scale Engine)
systems.licence: Proprietary; compiler not released as open source
systems.price_note: Cerebras Inference cloud API billed per-token; on-prem CS-3 systems sold/leased at enterprise pricing, not published
systems.model_formats: Accepts standard PyTorch/Hugging Face checkpoints; Cerebras' compiler statically maps the model across the wafer-scale core grid
systems.hardware_support: Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine (WSE-3) / CS-3 systems only — not deployable on any other hardware
systems.api_note: Cerebras Inference offers an OpenAI-compatible chat completions API on its hosted cloud
systems.runs_on: Cerebras CS-3 on-prem systems or Cerebras' own cloud
systems.best_for: Very high single-stream tokens/sec on large models, since wafer-scale on-chip SRAM avoids the memory-bandwidth wall GPUs hit
systems.watch: On-prem CS-3 system pricing is enterprise-quote-only and not published anywhere.
systems.benchmarks: Cerebras claims ~20x faster Llama 3.1 inference than GPU solutions at roughly a third of the power of a comparable DGX system (vendor-reported, not independently verified)
systems.verification_note: Performance figures are Cerebras' own blog claims versus GPU baselines; no third-party benchmark was located.

systems.name: MLX / mlx-lm
systems.price_note: Free and open source; fully self-hostable, no hosted fee or usage metering
systems.model_formats: Natively runs MLX-format models (safetensors-based weights converted from Hugging Face checkpoints via mlx_lm.convert, with optional quantization). GGUF support is EXPORT-only: mlx_lm.fuse --export-gguf converts a fused MLX model TO GGUF for use in tools like llama.cpp. There is no GGUF read/import path -- mlx-lm cannot load or run existing GGUF model files for inference.
systems.hardware_support: Apple Silicon via Metal is the primary and original target. The upstream ml-explore/mlx README also documents a Linux CUDA backend (pip install mlx[cuda]), newer and less mature than Metal, and a separate Linux CPU-only package (pip install mlx[cpu]).
systems.api_note: OpenAI-compatible HTTP server via mlx_lm.server (default port 8080), exposing /v1/chat/completions and /v1/models with streaming support. The server is explicitly documented as not recommended for production since it "only implements basic security checks."
systems.runs_on: macOS on Apple Silicon (unified memory) primarily; also Linux with an NVIDIA GPU via CUDA, or Linux CPU-only
systems.best_for: Local LLM inference and fine-tuning on Apple Silicon Macs, exploiting unified memory instead of discrete VRAM; increasingly usable on Linux too via the newer CUDA or CPU-only backends
systems.watch: GGUF is export-only -- mlx-lm cannot load or run GGUF model files, so the large existing GGUF/llama.cpp model library can't be reused directly; models must be MLX-format. Separately, the bundled mlx_lm.server is explicitly documented as not production-ready (basic security checks only), and prompt caching plus the large-model memory-wiring speedup both require macOS 15.0+.
systems.standout: The default way to get GPU-accelerated (Metal) LLM inference on Apple Silicon's unified memory architecture, with a large pre-quantized model catalog (mlx-community on Hugging Face) and an increasingly capable secondary CUDA/CPU Linux backend.
systems.architecture: Broad architecture coverage: Llama/Llama4, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma, Phi, Mixtral, DeepSeek, Cohere, Falcon, GLM, Mamba, and numerous MoE variants.
systems.multi_gpu: Distributed inference across multiple Apple Silicon machines via mlx.launch, using pipeline or tensor parallelism; on the CUDA backend, MLX can also use NCCL for multi-GPU/multi-node collectives.
systems.streaming: Yes -- mlx_lm.server supports token-by-token SSE responses on /v1/chat/completions
systems.context_note: Prompt caching (mlx_lm.cache_prompt) and the memory-wiring speedup for models large relative to available RAM both require macOS 15.0 or higher.
systems.quantisation: 4/6/8-bit affine quantization (default) plus mxfp4, nvfp4, and mxfp8 modes, applied via mlx_lm.convert -q; also supports mixed-precision recipes that vary bit-depth by layer/module.
systems.adoption: mlx-lm's own README states it "supports thousands of LLMs available on the Hugging Face Hub," and the mlx-community organization on Hugging Face hosts a large catalog of pre-converted/quantized MLX-format models.
systems.released: MLX framework: 2023-12-05 (Apple ML Research). mlx-lm as its own repository (the subject of this row): created 2025-03-11, after mlx-lm functionality was split out of the earlier mlx-examples repo.
systems.verification_note: Checked primary sources directly: mlx_lm/fuse.py and mlx_lm/gguf.py (confirms GGUF export-only, no import/load path), mlx_lm/SERVER.md, mlx_lm/convert.py argparse, LICENSE file (MIT, Copyright Apple Inc. 2023), GitHub API repo metadata (created 2025-03-11), ml-explore/mlx README (Apple Silicon/Metal primary plus Linux CUDA and CPU backends), mlx_lm/models/ directory listing.

gaps: No system in this edition other than vLLM and SGLang publishes a standardized, independently verified latency or throughput figure against a named test set — every other row's latency/throughput claims are either absent, a vendor's own unquantified description, or (LMDeploy, QServe, Cerebras, TensorRT-LLM, Mooncake, KTransformers, bitnet.cpp) a vendor-reported number that has not been independently reproduced, following the same discipline established on the Turns and Listening pages.

TensorRT-LLM and MLX / mlx-lm required a second, targeted re-research pass after the adversarial audit found the first-draft rows contained claims that were actively false. TensorRT-LLM's first draft asserted a mandatory ahead-of-time compile step (current docs show the PyTorch-native `trtllm-serve` path, no build step required, has been the default since v1.0) and an invented September 2024 relicensing date (the repo's initial commit is 2023-09-20 and its commit history shows no relicensing since). MLX's first draft claimed mlx-lm reads GGUF models (it only EXPORTS to GGUF, via `mlx_lm.fuse --export-gguf` — there is no import path) and that it is Apple-only (a newer, less mature Linux CUDA/CPU backend has since shipped), and cited the wrong upstream repo. The two rows in this edition are the corrected versions, independently re-verified against primary sources rather than the first draft's claims.

Ollama, KoboldCpp, and ExLlamaV2 were also researched during this edition's local and quant-specialist passes and put through the same adversarial-audit step every row above went through, with three different outcomes rather than one. KoboldCpp's row was rejected outright by the audit. Ollama's and ExLlamaV2's rows were not rejected — the audit notes that most of each row's content checked out — but each lost a required field to a claim the audit could not independently verify — Ollama's `model_formats`, and, among the four fields struck from ExLlamaV2's row (`facets`, `hardware`, `api_note`, `multi_gpu`), its `api_note`. This matrix requires all ten core fields to be present for publication, so both rows fell out of this edition despite surviving the audit's judgment on their other claims. All three remain candidates for a future edition — KoboldCpp if a corrected re-research pass can ground it in primary sources the way the TensorRT-LLM and MLX corrections above did, and Ollama and ExLlamaV2 if the struck fields can be independently re-verified.
